utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I notice that your client, Mr. Naletilic, was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes. He is not feeling very well. We have been informed that we have permission to continue with the proceedings in spite of his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just say something else to you? Not a single expert finding has been made, in spite of the decision you passed three months ago, believe it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think we will talk to the Registrar to look into this matter. And we only hope that your client will have a speedy recovery. Mr. Seric, are you ready for your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I am. The witness is outside, waiting to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any protective measures for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. This is an expert witness, an historian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we bring the witness, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Seric, would you permit me to ask you a question about the document that you presented to us that is the translation of Dr. Marijan's report. As a matter of curiosity, where was that translated? Can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our witness has a court translator in Zagreb, Professor Mario Maleta, so we have given this for a translation, and for that translation, we have had resources earmarked by the Registry of this Tribunal, because the translation of this expert opinion could not have been provided by the Registry in good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just curious to know whether it was translated here or elsewhere. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, I can hear you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You responded to the request of the Vinko Martinovic Defence team to elaborate an expert opinion on Bosnia-Herzegovina, everything that happened with that country that is nowadays a recognised state. However, before we start discussing this expert opinion of yours, could you please introduce yourself to the Court. Could you please give the Court your name and surname, and could you present your CV briefly.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: My name is Davor Marijan. I was born in 1966 in Prevlaka near Livno, Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have a degree in history and archaeology at the faculty of philosophy in Zagreb. I work in the Croatian Institute for History, and my project is the homeland war. Within that project, I have the duty to look at the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Croatian point of view. Let's put it this way, perhaps the history of the Croats in that area. So I'm dealing with problems related to war and soldiers. I am practically the only military historian in Croatia. I published two books, a third book is being published right now, and I've also published about ten scholarly papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the introductory part of your expert opinion, you talk about the war links between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, namely in the period between 1991 and 1995. In your opinion, what was Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Well, look, when you approach a time period that has just been completed, it is always difficult. First of all, not all sources are available; and secondly, in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is yet another problem: Many things happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina that are related to the disintegration of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina but I think that this is not completed in Bosnia-Herzegovina as such and that that hampers - how should I put this? - the reaching of well-founded conclusions. Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the present-day sense of the word, or rather, in that period of time, is a republic that was still in its inception. As the former Yugoslavia fell apart, Bosnia emerged within boundaries that it never had before. Its present-day boundaries are practically the republican boundaries from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, rather from 1947. And from 1945, of course, Bosnia-Herzegovina was part of this federation. It is the root or, rather, the root of such a Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina - at that time, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina - during the Second World War, that is to say at the session of the antifascist council of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Mrkonjicgrad, and formally that is how it was defined later, it was the state of Serb, Croats and Muslims. Rather it is not the state of Serbs, Croats and Muslims only but of all of them. From 1945 onwards, it was part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry to interrupt you, Witness. I think Mr. Seric should have warned you that whatever you say in this courtroom will be translated into the other two languages. We judges rely on the interpretation. So would you please make a pause after each sentence so that the interpreters could catch up with you. We have plenty of time - we have the whole week - so there is no need to hurry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I lost you really when you were saying that Bosnia-Herzegovina emerged as a country with boundaries that it didn't have before, and then you went flying into recent history and I think we lost you. Even though the translation was there, the mind can't keep up with it, so have a little pity on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the session of the antifascist council of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Mrkonjicgrad and the resolution or non-resolution of interethnic relations and resolving the national issue, the ethnic issue on that basis.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: All right. So in Mrkonjicgrad [Realtime transcript read in error "Konjic"], the future settlement of the interethnic issue was proclaimed, as it were. It says here "Konjic" but I really said Mrkonjicgrad. The problem is that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was a state that was not a free state, to put it mildly. So it was a state that, particularly during the first ten years, had a regime in power that was in fact a criminal regime. And in such a state, that proclaimed solution could have been maintained until 1990 while it was still a strong state, however, after 1990, that is to say when the Yugoslav crisis started escalating, this proved to be not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the other parts of the former Yugoslavia in the past?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: From 1945 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Seric please speak into the microphone; the interpreter did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Until 1945, Bosnia-Herzegovina did not exist under that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the interpreter warned us that she did not catch your question, Mr. Seric. Would you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can and I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What was the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina like and what was its status like as compared to the history period before 1945? Not only in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia but also before that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Well, from 1102, Croatia had a common state with Hungary. In about 1527 -- I mean, in that period, there was -- although this is a rather troublesome period of time, this is a time period that does not have sufficient written records. In that period, there is the banovina of Bosnia, which included the area a bit beyond present-day Sarajevo. So perhaps that is the only part when we can refer to some kind of relationship between two equal states. However, we are talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina here. Bosnia is one thing, Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think, is another thing. In the 15th century, the Ottoman empire conquered Bosnia, and Herzegovina, of course, and it remained under their rule until 1878. From 1878 until 1908, Bosnia-Herzegovina was a protectorate of the Austro-Hungarian empire. And in that period, it is defined in a way which resembles its present-day status. After 1918, Bosnia-Herzegovina became part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Or rather, from 1929 onwards, the state was called the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. In that period, sometime from 1922 onwards, all of Yugoslavia was divided up into new administrative units, nine banovinas. So at that time, none of the six communist republics that came into existence after the Second World War existed as such at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell this Trial Chamber, because we've heard different versions before this Trial Chamber - in all fairness, not everybody who spoke were experts - when was the Bosniak or Muslim nation created? I'm referring to the nation in the modern sense, the nations that were created, as we all know, in the mid-19th century. I'm speaking in that sense.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Well, in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, with the exception of Serbia, things were lagging behind as compared to Europe. Practically, it was the Muslims that were lagging behind the most, and from 1994, they were called the Muslim Bosniaks. The problem was the inheritance of the Ottoman empire. According to this inheritance, there was a distinction between people along the lines of religious affiliation, therefore, the term "Muslims," which actually denotes faith, however, from the Second World War onwards, the word was written with a capital M, Muslims. It can be said that the Muslims were quite divided amongst themselves. Part of them felt as Serbs or Croats and also the Serbs and Croats, on their part, tried to win them over to their side. As for the very name, "Bosniak," this is practically a product of the Austro-Hungarian empire. In the period during which, due to some misunderstandings between the Austrian and Hungarian parts of the empire, Bosnia-Herzegovina obtained special status. In that period, an attempt was made to link it to the Hungarian administrator, Benjamin Kallay, that is to say in order to create a unified Bosniak nation. Later on, in the 1990s, this project was repeated. From 1994 onwards, the term "Bosniak" re-emerged, which is a bit illogical because, in addition to Bosnia, there is Herzegovina. I personally believe that the process of creating the Bosniak nation has been completed and the last part of this was the war with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, we've heard here in this courtroom a few theses about the popular basis of the Bosniak nation, inter alia, that it stems from the Bogumils. What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The term "Bogumil" in the science of history was overcome in the 1950s. It is a term -- it is a term that was first used by Franjo Racki, a 19th century Croatian historian, because of the similarity with Macedonia where there was indeed a Bogumil movement or, rather, where Bogumils truly did exist. The term "Bogumils" was replaced by an historic term which appears in various sources. That is the term, "the Bosnian church," or "the Bosnian Christians." The term has been reintroduced now or, rather, in 1989 -- or 1990, to be more precise. It was reintroduced, so to speak, by Muslim or, rather, Bosniak scholars, none of whom had been dealing with medieval Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bosnia before. Obviously, the very term "Bogumil" suited their purposes better than the term "Bosnian Christians," for example. Their historiography that deals with this particular matter over the past few years is at the level of Croatia's in, say, the second half of the 19th century. It is too romantic a view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, let's move on now to modern history, recent history. What happened -- what kind of process evolved, at the moment or, rather, after the first multi-party and democratic elections were held in November, 1990?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: After these elections, the electorate, the entire body in Bosnia-Herzegovina was divided according to the ethnic principle. There were three ethnic groups, three nations, and their three national parties were supported by them respectively. Mr. Izetbegovic rightly says that the elections amounted to a census. The Croat Democratic Union, as a Croat party, practically advocated a view that was identical to the view expounded by the Croat Democratic Union in the Republic of Croatia. That is to say, a Yugoslav confederation. The Serbs advocated the thesis of a federal Yugoslavia, while the Muslim party, the Party of Democratic Action, supported the thesis about the indivisibility of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, it also promoted itself to the rank of the centre of -- for all Muslims for all of Yugoslavia. It wanted to become the centre for all Muslims in the former Yugoslavia, which was -- and the figure involved was about 6 million people. That is to say that they would rank third in terms of the population of all of Yugoslavia. So symbolically speaking, or to put it briefly, the Serbs and the Croats were looking at their original "homelands" so to speak, under quotation marks. I say "under quotation marks" because for Croatians, their home was really in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the western parts, and that can be established in the 8th and 9th centuries, whereas Muslims were looking at themselves, or perhaps to put it better, they were trying to attract all others towards them. That is to say, the approach that they espoused was contrary to the ones espoused by the Serbs and Croats respectively. The elections clearly showed that what was claimed before in terms of the interethnic issue was wrong, that is to say that it had been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, what were the views of these national parties with regard to the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: In essence, I think that the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina was viewed through the future of Yugoslavia. For the Croats, only a confederal Yugoslavia was acceptable, that is to say Bosnia-Herzegovina as a part of this confederal Yugoslavia. As for the Serbs, the view was in favour of a federal state. I already said that. And as for the Muslims, especially later in 1991, they came out with a platform meaning that Bosnia-Herzegovina could not remain in any common state where both Serbia and Croatia were not included, and by 1991, this had become absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship between Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only as a state but also as a space, so to speak? Or rather, what was its attitude towards the war that broke out in Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Well, look, let us say that the first element that came from Bosnia-Herzegovina was the question of territory. The first manoeuvre with the units of the Yugoslav army came through Bosnia-Herzegovinian territory, and that was in April and May, 1991. It was then that, from Pancevo via Prijedor -- Pancevo is in Vojvodina, rather, in Serbia -- a unit was brought, an armoured unit was brought to Petrinja, to Croatia. Also, an attempt was made with a JNA armoured unit from Mostar to get into Split. However, they didn't manage to do it. The Bosnia-Herzegovinian Croats stopped it at Siroki Brijeg. At the beginning of July, 1991, mobilisation was proclaimed in part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Within this mobilisation, in the area of Banja Luka, the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was mobilised, inter alia. In September, 1991, a large-scale attack by the JNA against Croatia took place, and parts of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina took part in it. Then also the reserve force of the JNA, most of them ethnic Serbs, also participated in this. Until the end of the war, this area was practically used as territory from which Croatia was attacked. So except for the main thrust of the attack that went from Vojvodina, all the other attacks came from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the Territorial Defence forces. At that time of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what is the Territorial Defence? What was the Territorial Defence then and what did it become later?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence at that time was part of the armed forces of the SFRY which, during the war, can be subordinated to the JNA, but of course in agreement with the Presidency of the country. The Territorial Defence was the question of the right of its mobilisation and usage or not, deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship of the Presidency, with Alija Izetbegovic at its top, towards the use of the units of the Territorial Defence in the war against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I think that the Minister of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina lodged a protest. But they remained at it. President Izetbegovic is always connected with the statement that it was not their war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I ask a question? [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Liu has very kindly allowed me to use his microphone. I wanted to ask two questions before we get too far away from it. When you say that the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was used mainly for attacks on Croatia, are you talking about the parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina which are now known as Republika Srpska? Could you be more positive in which areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina were being used to launch attacks? And secondly, I wondered why you as an expert historian, when you were asked what was the relationship of the Presidency with Alija Izetbegovic at its top towards the use of the units of the TO in the war against Croatia, answered, "I think that the Minister for Defence lodged a protest." Did he or didn't he? "I think" is not, in my submission, an appropriate word for an expert to be using to the Court. Either he did lodge a protest or he didn't. So there's two questions before we go too far.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the minister did lodge a protest. Another thing, most of the attack was the territory of the present Republika Srpska. The attack had been foreseen, had been planned across the western Herzegovina, but it did not take place because of the two-week mobilisation. The territory of the Bosnian Posavina - to be more concrete, of Bosanski Brod - was used for the manoeuvres of the Tuzla corps, which did not cross the river Sava, and a smaller tactical direction used went across via Bihac towards Slunj. That means that it wasn't only Republika Srpska but mostly it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, you started talking about the participation of all the three peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina; both Serbs, Croats and Muslims in the war in Croatia. Can you tell us how this participation -- what did this participation look like and how did it influence the relationship between these three peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The war against Croatia completed the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina into three confronted sides, or separate sides, which started with the elections. The Bosnian and Herzegovinian Serbs participated in the war in -- in that war in large numbers. As for the Bosnian and Herzegovinian Croats, after this expert opinion, after this expertise, I came -- I found data from 1993, to be honest, according to which, from the territory of Western Herzegovina, one part inhabited by Croatian which was called the assembly area, Tomislavgrad, and a smaller part of Central Bosnia, which was -- which means that around 3.500 people were in the police and the military of Croatia -- that is around 3.000 people which were within the Croatian Army, conscripts within the Croatian Army. And for the Bosnian Posavina and the Central Bosnia, I don't have any data. I wasn't able to find them. But I think that on the basis of this data, we could make some kind of evaluation around 4.000 or 4.500 people, which would make a nice brigade. As for the Bosnian Muslims, I actually quote a number. I didn't comment it, it was given by a retired person of the Muslim -- of the Croatian Army. He was a member of the Croatian Army. And he mentioned around 300.000 Muslims in the -- 30.000 Muslims in the Croatian war. So 30.000. I apologise. 30.000. For many years, I worked in the archives of the Ministry of Defence and I believe that this number has been multiplied at least six times. Part of Muslims, through the corps of officers, participated in the war in Croatia -- excuse me, against Croatia, and in any case, in that war, Bosnia was really divided according to the national principle. With the Muslims, there are still small deviations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What happened with this officers corps of the JNA who were the today's Bosniak -- of Bosniak nationalities after the war in Croatia had stopped?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This corps, mostly remained within the JNA until April of 1992, and from April -- since April, 1992, they started becoming part of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and later, into the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Their role was -- their role cannot be excluded when we discuss the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in order for us to be more concrete in connection with this historical period, what were the ambitions of the armed forces of JNA, of SFRY in relation to the Western Herzegovina, particularly in relation to Mostar and the Neretva River valley?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Veljko Kadijevic, the then national secretary or Minister of Defence, what we would say today, of SFRY, in his memoirs, gave a draft of the plan of attacking Croatia, and practically this was the arrival to the large Serbian line, the so-called Serbian line, Karlobag, Karlovac, Virovitica was the line. These were the areas where there were larger numbers of Serbs living. And the execution of that task, the problem of the complete eastern part would be solved, and that would have been Great Serbia. The operation did not succeed and of course then there was a reorganisation for -- reorganisation started for the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Because of the failure by JNA and the members of the then-called Krajina in Croatia, did it come to any change of war plans and war ambitions in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The period from January until April or May, 1992, is a period in which the Yugoslav army from the territory of Croatia came into Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in July or August, 1991, into the territory of Northern Bosnia and Herzegovina, as many as -- a larger part of the Maribor corps from Slovenia was pulled into. That was the time when various -- where members of the Serbian Democratic Party were armed, and there was a preparation -- there were preparations for a new war. In June of 1992, in Croatia, there was -- the United Nations forces gave up their line, the border, and that's how their hands were free to start the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that period, in May and June, 1992, the second military area of the armed forces of SFRY, the second military area of the armed forces of SFRY became the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, later, the Army of Republika Srpska. The 13th corps from Eastern Herzegovina, Eastern Herzegovina became its part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You said this morning that Bosnia and Herzegovina, as for the areas that it covers today in the same way, since 1878, that it remained as such, but can you tell us what the status was and has been until today?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I said that it was a more difficult thing. I think somebody else before me mentioned it. It is the question that outside its normal borders, there were -- the factor was always present which kept and took care of its wholeness, integrity. At some point, it was the Austro-Hungarian empire, and on the second occasion, it was the Communist Party of Yugoslavia. When it fell apart at the end of the 1990s of the 20th century, this balance was -- this balance disappeared. It did not exist any more. I quoted Mr. Zimmermann, the American ambassador, the then ambassador of the United States, whom Izetbegovic said that when Yugoslavia broke up, there was no destiny for Bosnia-Herzegovina either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When -- as we look at Bosnia and Herzegovina today and if we, as Judge Clark said, that Republika Srpska is considered to be a separate part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what is the position of today of the central government in relation to the parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. relation of the other two entities, as we usually -- as they are usually called?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I did not understand you quite well, but Bosnia and Herzegovina today, I said at the very beginning why that is a problem. Bosnia-Herzegovina is a divided country which consists of two entities which, as far as their independence is concerned, I wouldn't call them even federative. It is something more than that. And the protectorate of the international community prevents its disappearance and most probably a new war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the part before the conflict, prior to the conflict of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and HVO. How did it come -- let's talk about the war conflict and back to the first occurrences and war events. Was it something that took place very suddenly or had it been a process that took place?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Are you talking about the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I can call it the second phase of the war, because the first phase of the war was the war in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina cannot be excluded from it. It was a viewpoint that was predominant that the war begins at the moment when the most numerous people are endangered, which were the Muslims, and of course, that actually conflicts with the -- is against the thesis about the three equal peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You said that you would divide it into two phases and the first phase would be the war in Croatia. What was the position at the end of 1991 in relation to the war in Croatia and how this position then was transposed into Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: At the end of 1991, the situation was at a standstill in a way. The Croats could not launch a counterattack because they didn't -- they weren't strong enough for that, and the Serbs did not have the strength to continue. So the solution was the arrival of the international forces and of course the division, the separation, of course. During that time, the JNA slowly withdrew and was getting ready for the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and most officers of -- the later officers of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it must have been known, because they had been at the top of the army officials, army structures, and it was a surprise that they had not reported about it. Obvious -- they didn't report it to the members of the people that they belonged to, which was the case also with the Croatian officers, army officials, and it is not an unusual thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship of the national parties which won in the elections - so the Croatian Democratic Party, SDS, and SDA - towards this threat of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: All of them were illegally armed on the one hand, and Serbs already in the beginning of 1991 created a few autonomous areas, and afterwards, the Croats, in November, created the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croat community of Bosnian Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did discussions and negotiations on the future constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina start at an international level, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Practically, in the beginning of 1992, the so-called Cutilheiro Plan marked the beginning of such negotiations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, according to which it was supposed to be divided according to an ethnic principle, so to speak, and this is a permanent characteristic of all the policies that were pursued later by all the negotiating teams in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This policy culminated in August, 1993, in the Vance -- I think it was the Vance Stoltenberg Plan by then, about the union of republics in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The international community had already understood that and took the position that it was necessary to have a division along ethnic lines within the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is also a fact that is very important for looking into the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You said a short while ago that it was observed that all three parties were illegally armed and that they were practically preparing for war. In which way did this occur?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This was more or less organisation along party lines. According to what was made public, it was the Patriotic League as the military wing of the Party of Democratic Action, they started this sometime in June, 1991. The HVO, allegedly - when I say "allegedly," this is a later interpretation, I did not see any documents from that period - the HVO had some kind of tiny units in Western Herzegovina after the Uzice Corps came to the area of Mostar. And as for the Serbs, they went through the Territorial Defence practically from July, 1991, onwards. Part of them were waging war in Croatia. Recently - I found this literally a few days ago - there was some local commune from Bosanska Krupa, according to the principle of the SDS, it put itself at the disposal of Dvor Na Uni, that is -- that is in Croatia. So practically they made themselves availability to the Serb paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the establishment of the Patriotic League. Did you obtain any information, as you were working on archives, what was the programme like? What were the plans like? What did this Patriotic League have?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Practically, its first commander was most important for the Patriotic League. Sefer Halilovic, in his book which had several reprints described this. He presented part of the platform for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this shows that as for the enemies and destroyers of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he considers both the Serbs and Croats to be within their ranks. That is to say the extremist Croats, as he had put it. He did not make it clear -- he did not make it clear who he specifically had in mind when he said the "extremist" Croats. However, at any rate, this was already late in the winter of 1992. That is to say, March -- February, March, 1992, and of course, they it were poorly armed, like the HVO as well, after all. The Serb forces did not have any problems with weapons. I think that this has been documented quite extensively by now in several papers coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When was the military wing of the Croatian Defence Council founded and how?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: It was founded through a combination of some of the remnants of the Territorial Defence in that area, the reserve force of the police, and officially from the 8th of April, 1992, they came into being. The explanation was that the name was being changed because they could not take over the name of Territorial Defence because it had already earned itself a bad reputation. And finally by September, the Muslims also gave up on the words "Territorial Defence." They renamed it into the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the leaders of the Patriotic League came to head that army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What happened in the relations between the then Territorial Defence, later called the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the general staff of the JNA up until the moment when the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina declared a state of war?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: That is a period during which Mr. Izetbegovic, as President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, attempted or, rather, negotiated with the Yugoslav People's Army about its future in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These were his attempts for that army, this was practically the 2nd Military District, to be turned into the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course, that was an absurdity because it had already been transformed in part into a Serb army. Of course, these negotiations failed but they are interesting because of what Mr. Izetbegovic did. Actually, Mr. Izetbegovic demonstrated already at that stage his tendency to resolve the problems of Bosnia-Herzegovina elsewhere, as in Serbia, with general staff headquarters in Belgrade. And later on, problems with Croats or, rather, misunderstandings with Croats were being resolved with the Croats in Zagreb. In other words, he avoided contact with the Croats and Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't want to go into a new subject area. Can we perhaps take the break a bit earlier today and then proceed after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But Mr. Seric, this witness is an expert witness and we have already read his statement. So I think your job is only to draw our attention to certain points which you believe is very important to your case. We have spent about 75 minutes, but still we haven't come into the part which we are most interested in, that is, the Croats and the Muslim conflict. I hope after the break, we could come to that area as soon as possible. We'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, can you tell us in the briefest possible terms -- we are talking about the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you tell us about the first stage of the war between the Yugoslav People's Army and the Army of Republika Srpska on the one hand and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croat Defence Council on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, that first stage of the war is characterised by Serb attacks. When I say "Serbs," I'm actually referring to the Yugoslav People's Army until the end of May, the beginning of June, that is to say when it was turned into the Army of Republika Srpska. That period practically goes on until the end of 1992. And they try, through fast manoeuvres, primarily with armoured units, to take as much as they can. They acted very rapidly in Eastern Bosnia. They were successful. That has to be noted. In the area of Bosanska Posavina and in the area of Jajce, they had quite a bit of trouble before they attained their objectives and they did manage to do so in October, 1992. Their greatest failure was in Herzegovina in their attempts to take the banks of the Neretva River, but the Croat forces managed to repel them. In that period, the Croat forces were primarily engaged in defence. The same goes for Muslims. And their defence, although it was partly successful, was possible only because of the support of the Republic of Croatia. At the end of 1992, the intensity of the fighting waned and, later on, the campaigns became protracted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What were the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Croat Defence Council and, on the third side, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, towards the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992, the Serb army, the Army of Republika Srpska, was in the best position. It managed to resolve Bosanska Herzegovina because of their links with Serbia. In the area of Central Bosnia, it took Jajce and the hydroelectric power plants that were important for them. It kept Sarajevo and Bihac under siege. And out of its strategic plans, the only failure that they suffered was in Herzegovina. They did not get to the banks of the Neretva River, as I mentioned. The HVO managed to defend part of its territory where the Croats were a majority. At any rate, their greatest success was the defence of the Neretva River valley. As for the Muslim side, except for the defence of Sarajevo and Bihac, there were no major successes. However, in the case of Sarajevo, the Serb side already, in the summer of 1992, gave up on any rapid attempts to take it. It restrained itself to a rather strange tactical move of artillery siege and artillery strikes. The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was practically in the weakest position of all, and they had the least reason to be satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Because of the lack of military successes, they practically had no military victories.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What was the ratio between their manpower and the territory under their control?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: In that stage, that is to say in the summer of 1992, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established according to the JNA principle. It established five corps that were divided into manoeuvre and space structures respectively. The manoeuvre units were actually assault units, and, practically, later they were the protagonists of all the successes they achieved in the war with the Croats and to a far lesser degree in the war against the Serbs. As for the actual manpower level of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I'm not really sure. I cannot exactly say. I know that the commander of the 3rd corps, Hadzihasanovic, sometime in November, 1992, I think, claimed that he had 40 to 45.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: This is a very important question that has constantly been referred to throughout this trial: The attitude of the Republic of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Croatia towards the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: As for the attitude of the Republic of Croatia towards the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is reduced practically to giving assistance to the Croats, first and foremost, and also to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, namely the Muslims. When the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina entered its second active stage, so to speak, as opposed to the first passive stage, Croatia allowed the establishment of armed forces for the needs of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time, it was still the Territorial Defence. It allowed a trade in weapons and the establishment of training centres, and I think that this policy can be followed through documents until March, 1993. From then onwards, it probably stopped altogether, or rather it did stop altogether. Of course, assistance rendered to the Croats was bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Was there any intervention in terms of using the Croatian Army outside the boundaries of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: In my paper, I quoted an order from the 7th of July, 1992, I think, which prohibits the entry of Croat forces into other territories without explicit consent of the President of the Republic. I found another order - unfortunately I didn't bring it in - that dates back to sometime in March, 1992, the end of March, 1992. This order threatens that anybody who goes outside the borders of Croatia will be disarmed. I found it too late so I couldn't bring it. I'm talking about 1992, really. The Croatian Army is present in the border area with Bosnia-Herzegovina, primarily in the area of the southern front line, that is to say from the mouth of the Neretva River to Prevlaka. In the northern part, there is a bit in Posavina and the mentioned order of the Minister of Defence to a considerable extent affected the fall of Bosanska Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: The Croat-Muslim military cooperation and political cooperation, along which lines did it develop and how?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This cooperation, before 1994, before these accords that were reached through the mediation efforts of the United States, it is hard to say anything about it. There are some attempts up until that period, and according to these documents, the ones that I brought here, the ones I brought, they probably have the Republic of Croatia behind them. I already said, towards the end of the first part, that due to the policy of Mr. Izetbegovic to -- namely that he was avoiding the Bosnian Herzegovinian Croats and Serbs, although perhaps we can put it this way: On paper, through documents, they did not resolve this type of cooperation. There were no major conflicts. Well, there were conflicts but they were not large-scale conflicts, they are of local significance. The attempt to introduce order in these relations was the accord in Zagreb of the 21st of July, 1992, and specific attempts in military cooperation happened in November of the same year by creating a joint command, to which Slobodan Praljak was delegated from the Croatian side and Jasmin Jaganjac from the Muslim side. I have to admit that I didn't see a basis for this agreement. General Praljak told me personally that he himself did not see, let's say, any kind of legal basis for this agreement. So it seems that this could be reduced down to an oral agreement between Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic. Mr. Izetbegovic published his memoirs last year and in those memoirs he does not remember this agreement. And he doesn't remember a number of other things as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How did the political and military structures function in the areas where the percentage of Muslim and Croat population was the same?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I think that these were regions where the conflict broke out in later, these are regions where incidents occurred. But because of the Serb strategy, which we could call "scorched earth," in which practically after their conquests, nobody remained, the population either was taken to concentration camps or was expelled - for the most part it was expelled - very early on those regions lost their -- that characteristic of theirs because of a large in-flow of, in the first part, exclusively Muslim -- the Muslim population. So that we did not have an equal percentage of the population there any more. And a good example of this are Travnik, Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, and even in Mostar, a large number of Muslims arrived, which also changed the relationships in that area right away, creating -- constantly creating intolerance and laying the foundations for a future war. I think that in this book, "The Death of Yugoslavia," one of the ideologues from the Serbian side boasted about this strategy. I think it was Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: There is a prevailing opinion that the armed conflict, the war between the HVO and the Bosnian side, began precisely with the conflict at Prozor. What is your opinion about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. The conflict at Prozor is the first major clash, the first conflict which lasted for a couple of days -- the whole conflict lasted for a couple of days -- and it had larger consequences for a part of the local population. But with this conflict, several things are ignored. First, practically since April, 1992, until October, so for a full six months, each month you could identify minimum one conflict between the HVO and the Bosnia-Herzegovina TO, later the army -- Armija of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The biggest of those quote unquote, "minor" incidents, took place in September and October in Sarajevo, in the -- August and September, in the settlements of Otes and Stup. As far as the Prozor conflict is concerned, this is a conflict which almost certainly was not caused from a Croatian strategic source, and I'm thinking about the Croatian main headquarters. It happened during preparations of the Croatian forces, including the Croatian Army on the southern front, in order to take the area around Velez, Podvelezje, around Mostar. Immediately before this conflict, upon orders of the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, three 122-millimetre howitzers, out of a total of five or six that the operative zone northwestern Herzegovina had at its disposal, so they were -- the three were allocated to take part in this operation. In preparation for a conflict, this is not quite logical. By insisting on Prozor as the beginning of the war, or let me use the term Bosnian Muslim - i.e. Bosniak historiography - the way they phrase it, is the aggression of the HVO. Everything that happened later is amnestied. First of all, we are talking about March and April, in the area of Konjic and Jablanica. The Croatian state archives contain a large quantity of documents about the conflicts in Prozor and the area prior to that conflict, and the time period prior to the conflict, based on which you can see that the commander of the northwestern Herzegovina operative zone tried, by all possible means, to calm down the tensions which were constant in that area practically from the end of August. In spite of that, the conflict did break out, and ended with the defeat of the local Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Regarding that conflict, at some point in 1994, General Rasim Delic, in a speech before a meeting of Bosnian intellectuals, the council of Bosnian intellectuals, speaking about the conflict with the Croats, said that they had considerable problems in order to remove the HVO from roads, and I believe that that is the beginning of that project, which was successfully completed at some point in the autumn of 1993. I would also like to mention here the claims about the presence of the Croatian Army. Until today, I have not found a single document which would point to its presence, which was also confirmed to me by some of the participants. At the end, around Prozor itself, I think that this was construed by the agency for research and documentation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that is the Muslim or the Bosniak security service, AID, which the institute later, at the end of 1993, the Institute for the Research of Crimes of Genocide for the purposes of international law, documented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have tried not to be on my feet, as the Chamber will know, in the last couple of hours. But I think as we get closer to the core parts of what appears to be this witness's testimony, I want to state a couple of concerns. I realise, of course, that with any expert, there is a certain amount of background information which must be drawn on. However, I would understand from counsel that if counsel thinks that a particular point is important, presumably we would see the particular documentation and support for a position taken by the witness. In the last few minutes, for instance, there was one occasion where the witness said, "I've looked at thousands of documents at the state archives and this is what they mean." We don't know what documents he's talking about. None of those documents have been produced in court. Very difficult, obviously, for anyone - for either you, Your Honours, or for the Prosecution - to respond to "thousands" of anonymous documents. That's one concern. Secondly, just now, we were getting into, it seems to me, a bit argumentative when he talks about what some other government agency or some political party construed or didn't construe. So I simply want to state the Prosecution's concerns, Mr. President, as we get closer or into the core of this testimony, that while I understand he is an expert and has the ability to express some opinions, those opinions, we believe, should be supported in the Chamber on the record with the basis for those opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, the first issue is about the documents. If the witness claimed that he read a lot of documents to support his conclusion, that we would like you to ask some questions to this witness about those documents. Secondly, Mr. Seric, you may ask some particular questions so that -- to dispel the doubts from the Prosecution side concerning the government involvement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: My microphone is now working. But about five minutes ago, Mr. Seric, when we were approaching the core issues in relation to the background of the conflict between the HVO and the Muslim armed forces, we were talking about the genesis of the war, and your expert was explaining to us that it was a mistake to take Prozor as the starting point. We are going back as far as there, and I was following carefully the translation. He then went on to deal with preparations by the Croatian forces in the attempt to take the area around Velez, and you mentioned -- or he mentioned a lot of places which we are not necessarily familiar with. So it wasn't clear to me whether this joint effort was taking part in the area of the Republic of Croatia or in Herzegovina. And also, it was not clear to me whether he was talking about the HV or the HVO or both because the translation, to me, suggests that it was a joint effort between the HV and the HVO to take the territory in the area around Velez. I was going to interrupt at that point and then I thought maybe if I keep quiet it will become clear, but it isn't becoming clear. Is there any way that we can distinguish in the translation between Croatian forces that we know as HV and Croatians who live in Bosnia-Herzegovina? There is a problem and it's very unclear, so perhaps you could ask a question -- well, perhaps maybe I could ask the expert a question. Can I ask you, when you were dealing with the events following Prozor, when you were talking about the -- what sounded like a joint effort to retake or to take lands around Velez and various other places that you mentioned, are you talking about a joint effort between the HVO and the forces of the Croatian Army from Croatia, or are you talking -- or what are you talking about? Because now we are approaching, obviously, the important part of this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this: I would like to correct the Prosecutor. I did not say that I reviewed 1.000 documents about the conflict in Prozor but I said that I did review many documents. That is not the same. As far as the situation in taking up the Velez area, this was the first Mostar Brigade and the -- and HVO forces. And there was another, also, brigade which took part in that operation but it did not have much success. The Croatian Army did its part of the operation on the other side of the border. So it was a joint operation which, on the Bosnia and Herzegovina side, the focus was on the units of the HVO with participation of the units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, you see that's the problem. As you and Mr. Seric can talk very quickly about towns and villages on either side of the border, we don't know that. So if you could say, when you're dealing with a town, where its location was, or even if we were referred to a map so that we could realise that there was a backup force on one side of the border and a joint force on the other, but it certainly wasn't clear to me that the Armija was involved in the joint forces or that the Croatian Army was on the other side of the border. And these things are important because it sounded to me as if you as an expert were giving testimony of the involvement of Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, what's the problem, Mr. Krsnik? I think Judge Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Clark has stated --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to be clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have anything to add, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must say that recently I have been surprised by your reactions when I stand up. Do you think that the Defence of Mladen Naletilic has nothing to do here any more? I would be happy if that were the case but this is a very important witness about very important general facts regarding the indictment. I just wanted to object and respond to the objection by the Prosecutor, which I consider quite inappropriate because everything that the Prosecutor said, they will have the opportunity to say that in the cross-examination and the cross-examination in this procedure here is the way to throw a doubt into the testimony of this witness. You cannot use these arguments to interrupt the examination-in-chief, the way it was done by Mr. Scott a little while ago. This is what I wanted to say, and I think that I'm absolutely in the right, and knowing the way Mr. Scott works, it is absolutely clear to me that as soon as topics that he does not like are touched upon, then he interrupts the witness and turns the topic to where it suits him. That is the gist of my objection. And I believe that this is something that he should not be allowed to do. That is precisely why there is a cross-examination. So he does have the right to question about the documents the witness has looked at, where, when, and what these documents are. That is the purpose of the cross-examination, Your Honour. So this is what I wanted to say. Thank you very much. And this witness, absolutely I could call him a common witness because he's testifying about important aspects of the indictment, even though I did not have the opportunity or the honour to talk to this witness prior to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think we have to judge the intention of the Prosecution with bona fides because, in our view, that the Prosecution raised these issues just to help the Chamber and help Mr. Seric to conduct his direct examination. Sometimes we couldn't know whether that is a fact or is the opinion of this witness. So at minimum, we need some documents to support the view expressed by this witness. I think that is a legitimate request and it will help the proceedings of it trial. Well, Mr. Seric, would you give -- would you please give more lead to this witness concerning with those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to say now that at this point, nobody assisted me or offered any help but they are just doing quite the opposite. For me it is confusing. First I was told to go faster because you had the expert report. When I did start to go faster, now I'm being asked to go more slowly. Now the Prosecutor is interrupting, and my colleague, Mr. Krsnik, is absolutely right in saying that this is not an appropriate type of objection but a kind of personal observation, so a criticism of the expert testimony which we have not heard to its end. So I myself, as the Defence counsel of my client and as leader of the team, should be able to have a least a minimum of initiative in the way I'm carrying out this examination-in-chief. I respect your instructions that the witness should back up his arguments by appropriate documents, but -- I'm not completely lost, I can't say that, I'm not that kind of person, but I am confused. Let us permit the expert witness to say what he means to say, and of course, I will lead him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness, what was this all about? On one side we have long-standing -- a thesis that this was a natural alliance between the Bosnian Croats and Muslims, and then on the other hand we have these events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This claim about natural allies would be worth accepting had it been realised at the point of aggression against Croatia in 1991. This natural alliance did not exist at all at that time. In other words, it was supported by those who saw the crucial part in Bosnian Muslims and who based their opinions on their opinions. Alliance by logic in difficult circumstances. In 1991, the Republic of Croatia was threatened as well as a good many -- number of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I did not see any indications that Mr. Izetbegovic as President of the Party of Democratic Action on one side, and then also as President of the Presidency, tried to do anything in order to work on this problem. This is a thesis which was construed later, by which they also wish to say -- well, in 1992 both Croats and Muslims did have a common enemy but they did not have a common purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So essentially, why was this war waged?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Mildly speaking, this was a war over territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What does that mean? Was somebody lacking territories?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The Serbs launched it, which is interesting, even though, by numbers, they are second. At the end of 1992, they had about 70 per cent of Bosnia, which was too much for the number of the population. And later, others joined in. The Croats held their own. They held the main areas where they were the majority and parts of the Central Bosnia areas where they numbered more or less the same as the other populations. Of course, there were slight deviations from that. Later, the international community joined in with their plans of division and thus the Croatian areas were treated -- Konjic and Jablanica were also treated as Croatian areas, as well as Stolac, where Muslims were a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When analysing documents and literature, and various writings that pertained to this conflict between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO, did you analyse the participation of the Croatian state in this war, notably from the following aspect, that Croatia was an aggressor against Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Well, you see, in the documents that I reviewed in the Croatian state archives, and these are HVO documents and there are also some Serb and some Muslim documents as well. As far as I know, it is accessible to the Prosecution as well, with the approval of the government of the Republic of Croatia, which I did obtain in order to access this. There are documents in which the presence of the Croatian Army can be noted from mid-1993 in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I mentioned a few such documents here. I think that I did not find only one there. Only one of them I did not find there, which is no surprise in view of the time I spent there - about 120 working hours, that is - and I reviewed about 350 binders that pertain to strategic and operational levels. As for this period, that is to say from July, 1993, until May, 1994, in the area of the operative zones of southeast Herzegovina, and northwest Herzegovina, there was a Croatian Army presence or, rather, there were soldiers from the Croatian Army that were present there. Documents speak of this. These are units that are considered to be units of volunteers. If there is perhaps any doubt in terms of some units that were of the professional type, there are no such doubts with regard to units belonging to the reserve force. It was impossible to deploy them without their voluntary consent. I wish to draw your attention to the following, that Bosnian and Herzegovinian historiography and other writings that I've been following for years, primarily uses the term "brigades." Both Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, all the armies in the territory of the former Yugoslavia accepted the term and meaning of "brigade" from the Yugoslav People's Army. A brigade is a higher tactical joint unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: On the Bosniak side, were there any fighters from abroad who were engaged?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Practically from the summer of 1992, in the area of Central Bosnia, one could identify fighters or, rather, volunteers from Islamic countries that were in this area. In this area and beyond, they have been called the mujahedin. I think that an HVO document mentions them sometime in August, 1992, in Travnik, and the figure of about 700 men is actually referred to. The final estimates vary, that their numbers grew to several thousands. However, these are primarily figures coming from the newspapers or from the Croat or Serbian sides. That means that degree of caution should be authorised, some reservation, but that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, from a professional point of view, as a military analyst, in view of the war of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what position would you take? I am primarily referring to the conflict between the Serb side on the one hand and on the other hand the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croats, and then in addition to that, the war that occurred between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: We can say that 1992, denoting the first stage, involves attacks by the Serb side in order to take the territory that their ideologues considered to be their own. After that, in 1993, there was a war of all against all. As for the Muslim side, the Bosniak side, there are elements of civil war. Nowadays, we have a major problem pertaining to this war, and I think that there is no answer to it, and I believe there won't be an answer soon, and the problem is how should this war be called? The Muslim Bosniak historiography and other writings, both those from the time of war and contemporary writings as well, when meaning the Serbs, when writing about the Serbs, they write about the Serb Montenegrin aggressors. "SCA" is the abbreviation used. I personally consider this to be absurd. And that was perhaps tenable until the summer of 1992. As for the Croats, when they are referred to, they refer to the aggression of the Croatian Army. And the part of the HVO that they waged war against they call fascists. This is all too reminiscent of communist rhetoric in the former Yugoslavia. That is going to be a big problem, how -- what to call this war, how to consider involvement in it. I personally see this war evolving in three circles: In the first circle is Bosnia-Herzegovina, with three peoples and three armies. In part, they are waging war two against one, all against all, and again two against one. That is the part until the war stopped. The second circle would be practically the countries surrounding Bosnia-Herzegovina, namely Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. They undoubtedly gave military and financial assistance on the one hand to their compatriots, and in the case of the Republic of Croatia, to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. Finally, there is the third circle. That is the international community. We can see its traces starting with the ban on weapon imports in the former Yugoslavia in 1991. We can see it through 1992, that is the peacekeeping forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It exists in order to eliminate part of the theatre of war, namely the air. And finally, it is involved in combat operations against Republika Srpska or namely the Army of Republika Srpska. However, there is a big problem involved here to give it a more precise name. On the one hand, these are big powers or, rather, influential circles, influential political circles, that influence the Security Council that adopted various binding resolutions, but on the other hand, there is also the public opinion in these countries, which, after various images from the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina went round the world, affected the change, the partial change, in the policies of their countries towards that war. Of course, in relation to the second circle here, it is very hard to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, you brought along a series of documents that we distributed to all parties in the courtroom. You have copies in front of you. You brought two documents just when you arrived so we did not manage, Your Honours, to have them translated yet. We are now going to look at this in order. The first document, the 15th of November, 1991, is its date. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to the honourable Judge Diarra; we were not in a position to ensure a translation into French. As for our colleagues in the Prosecution, we did not manage to do this in chronological order but, Mr. Scott, we do have a copy for you in chronological order, so perhaps it would be of assistance. I think that, Madam Registrar, this document will be D2/59 or perhaps later. Well, all right, D2/59.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So what does this document say to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This is a selection of documents. I personally wish that all the documents I referred to, quoted, were in there. All right, but this document related to the -- dated, rather, the 15th of November, 1991, is proof of the presence of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the war against Croatia. That is the first document that I found. The original itself is in the counterintelligence agency of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What about the next document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Let me say what I have to say for the transcript. It is dated the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 7th of April, 1992, so it would be D2/60. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This document is General Spegelj's document, and he was chief inspector of the army of the Republic of Croatia. He requests the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Susak, to approve the sending of a unit of about 1.200 men - for the most part Croats and Muslims, or to be more precise, Muslims and Croats - to Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to engage in war there. This document is the beginning of a unit called the 7th Krajina Brigade. This is just an addition. After the fall of Jajce, this brigade was linked up to the 1st Krajina Brigade, which, in May, 1992, left Zagreb. This was later the 17th Krajina Brigade, an elite unit of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Muhamed Alagic was its operation officer. Mehmed Alagic, I beg your pardon. The next document --

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Let me just say that it is the 8th of April, 1992. It would be D2/61.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This document confirms the possibility of volunteers from the Croatian Army going outside the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: The next document would be dated the 9th of April, 1992, so it would be D2/62. My question is what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This document is a confirmation of the document dated the 7th of April, and the Ministry of Defence granted the request put forth by the chief inspector of the Croatian Army. Let me just mention one thing: These three documents are in the office of the Minister of Defence and in the appropriate department of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: My question pertains to the next document, the 10th of April, 1992. It would be D2/63. What does that mean? What does it represent?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: It is approval for arming the Croatian Muslim party, and it is signed by the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: The next document relates to a document also dated the 10th of April, 1992. It would be D2/64.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Practically it is the same thing. The same thing can be said as for the previous document, that is to say, help to the Muslim population, and it comes from the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now my question pertains to the following document. It is dated the 14th of May, 1992, and the number would be D2/65. What does it mean? What does it support? Which thesis of yours?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The thesis of Croatia's assistance to the Muslims. Specifically, this involves a colonel, no mention is made of where, but in view of northern Posavina, it is the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: The next document that my question pertains to is the same nature. It is dated the 7th of July, 1992, and the number would be D2/66.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This is the order, the instructions that I already commented upon, the ban on units leaving the territory of the Republic of Croatia. It's issued by the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I would like you to look at the next document. It is the 28th of July, 1992. Its number would be D2/67. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This document is a concrete example of assistance to the armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is the defence staff of the municipality of Kalesija, near Tuzla, somewhere around Tuzla, and towards the bottom of the page, the head of the main staff of the HVO allowed passage of the convoy. As for this type of document, I would like to say one thing: In contemporary Muslim writings and historiography, when such a document is found and it's published as a facsimile, if assistance is given by the Croatian Defence Council, then that is proof of aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina committed by the Republic of Croatia. That is what they call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the next document, dated the 25th of August, 1992. It is going to be number D2/68.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The same as the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: The next document is dated the 12th of October, 1992. It's going to be number D2/69. Please tell us, how do you explain this? What does it pertain to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: It is also a document that refers to the assistance of the Republic of Croatia to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The military attache of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a man who was the first commander of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, authorises a general of the Croatian Army, Mate Sarlija, to collect aid for Bosnia-Herzegovina. I just have a brief comment to make. Mr. Efendic, Mr. Efendic wrote a book about his participation in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and his views thereon. He does not remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: My question now pertains to the next document, dated the 28th of February, 1993, D2/70. What does it represent? How do you explain it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: It says the 26th of February here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Oh, the 26th of February? Oh, I misspoke, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This is also a continuation. This speaks of the time when assistance is continued to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I think that we should slow down with our questions and answers. Perhaps you should start answering my questions after I finish putting the question. So could you please look at the next document and tell us what it means. It is dated the 6th of March, 1993, and it would be number D2/71. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This is also a document about the assistance by the Minister of Defence for the B and H army, and a list is given here of persons who are responsible for the transport and also the licence plates of the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now we have a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we don't have a translation. We can put the document on the ELMO if Mr. Marijan would like to quote some passages from this document. We will place the document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 13th of March, 1993. That will be document D2/72.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, the things that you consider important, please tell us, and read so that the interpreters can follow you as well as the monitor.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This is a very interesting document. It's quite unusual since it was written by the commander of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we don't have a signal back here. Mr. President, it started out, we had it, and then it's just blank, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, soon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they cannot see it either any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since we have some technical problems, my suggestion is that we break now and let the technicians fix the equipment so that it will smooth the proceedings. By the way, Mr. Seric, we don't have that D2/72 in our hands. Maybe during the break you could furnish us with that document, even if it's in B/C/S. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, we left off with this document, D2/72, which is on the ELMO right now. Could you please explain to us what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This is a document sent by the 4th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, its command. Judging by the signature, this is probably the signature of Sulejman Budakovic, the Chief of Staff, to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. Two things are important here. One, you can see from the document regarding the earlier certificates about help to the army of B and H, that the HVO was stopping convoys, both those that were transporting weapons and let's say humanitarian convoys, and humanitarian convoys, but I'm quoting: "After our intervention, the large -- a large number of equipment was returned." The other thing is that the commander of the corps or the person who signed on behalf of him says: "The HVO --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "And this has been implemented, which is useful for the Muslims, [as interpreted] and certificates are required from the republican MUP." I obtained this document from private hands, the original. It's a different document. It's from the instruction and training section of the corps, meaning that the source should be looked for in the archives of the President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself, the previous sentence was "devastating for the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a little bit unusual for the commander of the corps to be addressing himself directly to the President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Let's move to the next document, from the 20th of March, 1993. It should be D2/73. I will give the document to the usher to place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This is a document signed by --
