utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: On page 45, line 14, 15, the witness was speaking and then the interpreter asked that -- I'm sorry, I'm sorry, it's up a little further, page 45, line 8, the witness was answering, "The HVO --" the interpreter said could the witness please read more slowly, and it appears there is some interpretation missing. Starting again on line 10. I think that we missed part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much to draw our attention to that point. Mr. Seric, would you please clear that up for us. Page 45, line 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, Your Honour. I would like to find it. I don't see it on the screen any more. I just need to find it on the computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Seric, I don't know if you've noticed that I'm talking over to Judge Liu. I don't know if I'm the only one in court but I have not the slightest idea what that document purports to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could you please be kind enough to have this document translated today so that, during the cross-examination, we could have the English copy? Otherwise, we are just in total darkness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will try to do that, Your Honour, but let's -- in order to hear the answer completely, we will return the document just so that we can hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I would recommend that the following document should be translated as well, the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Minutes?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: It's practically a confirmation that Sarajevo took steps at the suggestion of the command of the 4th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is a document which also specifies certain things, amongst other things the taking of the Zlatar facility in the region of Konjic. Specific weight is given to the document by the commanders of the -- by three commanders of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the commander of the municipal command of Jablanica, the commander of the battalion of the military police of the 4th Corps, and, three, -- and three signatures of the chiefs of police stations. Another important thing about this document is that the HVO got it two or three days later and practically these two documents go -- are part of the core set of documents which caused the war between Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: We will come back to the previous document now. Could the usher please place that on the ELMO? For the transcript, which is incomplete, in part, we are now talking about document D2/72. Could you please repeat what you said about this document.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This document is interesting for two reasons. One, it confirms that the HVO, or it practically confirms previous documents based on which you could see military assistance sent from the Republic of Croatia or the Ministry of Defence, to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the HVO took a part of the equipment but most of it, it did allow to pass through. The other part is because of the introduction of Herceg-Bosna licence plates, steps be -- certain steps be taken by Sarajevo, from Sarajevo, and then seven days later, this -- these minutes are a confirmation that steps had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. We are now moving to the document of the 30th of March, 1993, which is D2/74. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is another document about the assistance that was given. This is probably -- this is certainly the final stage of these transactions. They stopped in April the same year. So they stopped the next month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: At this same time, covered by these documents and particularly the 30th of March, 1993, were there any conflicts between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Conflicts came later. Specifically, in the second half of March. So since this document, until the 30th of March, there were conflicts in the region of Konjic and Jablanica, which brought us into the -- into mid-April of the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: The next document of the 18th of April -- April, 1993, will be number D2/75. What does this document show?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This is a combat report of the B and H army. I'm not quite sure what unit this is. This is probably one of the local brigades. According to the command of the 4th Corps, based on which we can see, let's say, the rhetoric of the army -- of the B and H army. We are talking about liberation operations, specifically for Zlatar, which was the communications centre. It was taken, captured during the day. Earlier here we saw a -- and I pointed out to the minutes of the 20th of March, where this was covered, foreseen. There is a sentence here that says, "The villages of Vucari and Vrbovici, being the HVO strongholds, have also been seized today, liberated today." As I've already said, this illustrates the kind of rhetoric the -- where the enemy is in a majority and this is called liberation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Are these attack operations, assault operations?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you please concentrate on the sixth paragraph of this document, which begins, "At this moment..."

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: "At this moment, brigade Neretvica is liberating the HVO strongholds of Pokariste and Cerici. This will bring the complete right bank of the Neretva under our control."

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next document, dated the 8th of June, 1993, which will be number D2/76, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This document is trying to suppress quite a widespread claim about ethnically cleansed single-ethnic units in the HVO. The biggest percentage of such units were in the operative zone of East Herzegovina, especially in the 1st Brigade of the HVO, the Capljina Brigade, and particularly in the 2nd and 3rd HVO Brigades in Mostar. On the 30th of June, 1993, because of treason and their move to the side of the B and H army, the Sjeverni Logor Northern Camp barracks fell. This document gives us the percentage of Muslims in the operative zone northwestern Herzegovina, where we can see that in the Rama Brigade in Prozor, so eight months after the conflict in October, 1992, you practically have almost a quarter of the unit which is comprised of Muslims, and also for the Petar Kresimir Brigade from Livno, you have a similar ratio. Central Bosnia, for the most part, does not have such mixed units. The units there are really ethnically pure, and there are percentages, in other places, of Muslims in HVO brigades. I would now like to focus on the B and H army. The only -- the headquarters of the Supreme Command are multi-ethnic there, so at the strategic level. Mr. Izetbegovic, in his memoirs which were published last year, published a letter from one of the deputy commanders, deputy chiefs of staff, Mr. Jovan Divjak, a Serb by ethnicity, from which you can see that he had been completely marginalised and that his role was purely decorative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: My next question, Mr. Marijan, relates to the document of the 10th of June, 1993, and it will be numbered D2/77. What does this document mean to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This document talks about the aid offered by the Croatian air force, both to the HVO and to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for medical purposes. So purely for humanitarian purposes. And it talks about the problems encountered, being encountered in that process or in these attempts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And the last document in this set is from the 10th of July, 1993, and it will be number D2/78. What is this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This document is basically an expression of thanks signed by the Tuzla -- the commander of the 2nd B and H corps from Tuzla to the commander of the 4th HVO operative zone in Bosanska Posavina, in which he is thanked for the artillery support that was given. At that time, the war in the other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the war between the B and H army and the HVO, had totally escalated by that time, which also speaks of the impossibility to reduce the picture to a simple, uniform one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Please, and let us finish with that, could you please read the third passage.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: You mean, "Required"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note we don't have the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "It is necessary to continue in this way and in this way to help our defence, or to defend Bosnian Posavina as the symbol of our common defence, the Croats and the Muslims, for a unified state of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And who signed this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The commander of the 1st operative group of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the 2nd corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours, I have finished my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, do you have any questions to ask, or do you believe that Mr. Seric has successfully exhausted all your questions in your mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have some questions, questions which I believe are lacking some explanations or clarifications in the answers because I carefully followed the questioning of my learned friend Mr. Seric and I followed the transcript. I don't think that I will need a lot of time, but I believe that some things need to be clarified for you also, Your Honours, so I will strictly stick to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to introduce myself, Mr. Expert. My name is Kresimir Krsnik, I'm a lawyer from Zagreb, and I am the Defence attorney of Mr. Naletilic who is not present here right now. I would like to put to you a few questions in order to get some clarifications from you. Especially because I hadn't had the honour before of talking to you so I will refrain from asking more detailed, other questions. First of all I will start with the question which was put to you by my learned friend Mr. Seric regarding Prozor as regards this being taken as the date of so-called conflicts between the Bosnia-Herzegovina army and the HVO. And you, in a part of your answer, said the following: "That in the Bosniak or Muslim modern historiography, this was being publicised and fabricated in order to amnesty what happened later." So could you please clarify to the Court what it was that happened, what is it that they wished to amnesty? And dear sir, I would like you to mention dates and years, absolutely, of these events, and to speak slowly, please, because of the interpretation. And please describe that area. In a part of your answer you mentioned Stup, the municipality of Stup, in Sarajevo. Of course we from that area here are familiar with the towns and the municipalities but please be aware of the fact that in this courtroom, it is only we who know that, but there are other people who come from different countries and who would perhaps require an explanation of these terms. Perhaps my question was a little too long, but my basic question is what did you mean when you said, "To amnesty what happened later"? First, what is it that happened, where did it happen, and when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I primarily meant these two documents here, which have, unfortunately, not been translated yet. The documents which relate to the upper part of the Neretva River, so this is the area of Konjic and Jablanica, where at the end of March and the beginning of April, or from the end of March and the beginning of April, 1993 - better put it like that - we have a conflict between the Croats and the Muslims. These documents confirm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise. I have another question. Who is attacking at the end of March and the beginning of April in the Konjic area?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Assault attacks are being -- assaults are being carried out by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which can be seen from this report of the 18th of April, 1993. In this way, as I said before, when you begin with Prozor, then you amnesty all that happened later, because the beginning of the war is located there. After that, nothing else is important. It's just war. I quoted that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I honestly can't follow it because it may be a question of translation. "Amnesty" is not a verb in English so I don't understand why a thesis is promoted in order to amnesty. What is the real meaning of to amnesty; to cover up, to forgive? It's being used as a verb and I don't believe "amnesty" was ever a verb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it is better to say to conceal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: To conceal and to justify, that is what "to amnesty" means in our language, to conceal or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: "Amnesty" in English has a completely different meaning. To conceal. Okay, I can live with conceal because then it has some logical meaning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be best, in the spirit of the language - of course, I will not interfere; we have quite qualified staff here - but perhaps it would use it for what happened later.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is justification. The book by Mr. Smail Cekic "Aggression Against Bosnia and Herzegovina, The Genocide Against Muslims and Bosniaks," from 1994 -- I think that you just need to read it in order to see what this gentleman is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, could you tell us in a few words, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I think that this book probably served to -- or which was probably created following the complaint by Bosnia-Herzegovina against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which I was confirmed -- which was confirmed to me by a person who actually did most of the work on this. And this first part of the book, which is very, very good, I have to admit that, was partially -- the part against the Serbs was based on documents of the Yugoslav People's Army. The second part, which relates to the HVO or, as he calls it, the fascist part of the HVO, was mainly based on intelligence estimates of the B and H army, which were bad. Amongst other things, the thesis was accepted about the attack of the 113th Split force, the 114th Sibenik, and the 123rd Varazdin brigades of the Croatian Army against Prozor and Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please just clarify this briefly to the court, Sibenik, Varazdin, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. These units do exist in the Croatian mobilisation establishment. However, the 113th is from Sibenik. The 114th is from Split. The 123rd is from Slavonska Pozega, and I think that these two or, rather, the 123rd was transformed then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: It is one that is supposed to recruit conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please follow the cursor on the monitor, and when it stops, only then start answering; is that all right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Such units are not used for combat operations, generally speaking. Let us leave aside the fact that in documents of these units, there are no designations in terms of them operating down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What does "down there" mean?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the 114th Brigade or, rather, one of its platoons was, towards the end of 1993, in the area of Prozor but not at the end of 1992. This platoon, not the entire brigade. A platoon involves 25 to 40 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please say the following: Whether you know the date and year, in terms of events going on in Central Bosnia and what is going on in Sarajevo. Actually, I would like to put the following to you: What you said by way of evidence before this Trial Chamber today, the terminology from Bosnian historiography is absolutely being used by the Prosecution in this Court.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: That is what I noticed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please just pause for a minute. I have a concrete question. In the indictment that we have, and I have seen others as well, there is the date of the 16th of April, 1993, as the beginning of the attack launched by the HVO and the HV against Muslims, that is to say citizens of Muslim ethnicity, and it is being claimed quite innocently that at first they were all unarmed. That is to say, the 16th of April, 1993. Can you tell this honourable Trial Chamber, and you already have told them to a large extent, so let's go back now chronologically. The 16th of April, 1993 and let us move back to the end of 1992. Where did conflict take place? Who was the attacker? And what was involved?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The beginning of 1993, there was a conflict in Gornji Vakuf. That is the area that could be called the south of Central Bosnia. That is the area above Prozor, which, towards the end of the month, spread to Central Bosnia as well, notably Busovaca. This conflict took place after a round in the Geneva negotiations. While in the territory of Gornji Vakuf, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina accepted the demand put forth by the HVO for the 305th Mountain Brigade of the BH Army, consisting of military age refugees from Jajce, which was brought in in December, 1992, to this area, be returned to central Bosnia. This is an interesting example of upsetting - how shall we put this? - this ethnic balance on the one hand, and on the other hand, this military balance, and it seems that the HVO was particularly sensitive to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So let us draw a conclusion. How many conflicts and who was the attacker until the 16th of April, 1993? If you can mention all of this.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This conflict in Vakuf, then this conflict in Busovaca, and particularly in southeastern Herzegovina, there is ongoing tension after that, and ultimately these attempts by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina towards the end, when they launched a process, if we can put it that way, of eliminating the HVO in the area of Konjic and Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Ah, Konjic and Jablanica. Can you tell the honourable Trial Chamber on which date the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina attacked the HVO or, rather, non-Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I think it was the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know of the fate of this area, what happened to the non-Muslims from Konjic to Jablanica or, rather, from Konjic to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I think that in this area, as far as I know, a few war crimes were committed. In addition to the military commanders, a certain Safet Cibo is accused of that. On the 20th of March, 1993, he was appointed, let us say, the person in charge for these areas, Konjic and Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to say the following: Until the 16th of April, 1993, what were the objectives of the BH Army, or rather the SDA? What were their real objectives? And how did they portray them to the world?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Could you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What did the BH Army want to do with these attacks until the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: As for these attacks specifically on Konjic and Jablanica, that can all be seen from these minutes. This is an attempt to eliminate, and it's a successful attempt at that, to eliminate the military and political authorities of the HVO. This is the struggle for roads and communications, and they were also successful in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You said at one moment that it is clear from the documents, from the reports, that the BH Army is liberating certain places, certain areas, and you said that was absurd. It sounds absurd to me as well. Who was it liberating it from?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: From the autochthonous population and the members of the Croatian Defence Council, that is to say, the military wing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell the honourable Trial Chamber in this terminology that the Prosecution in this Court uses, the term was used very often, of course, until we gave some other pieces of information, they used the term "government forces." What does that mean in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, 1993, the government authorities? Witness, please, I don't want to lose any of your valuable testimony so please slow down.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I can say that we are entering the domain of something that is called law here, and I'm a historian. So I can give you my opinion about that. Perhaps I can indicate some things that seem illogical to me as an historian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please speak as an historian, not as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Well, I cannot speak as a lawyer. The fact is that Bosnia-Herzegovina, towards the end of 1990, got this -- how shall I put this, this strange tripartite government authorities. That is to say that it was according to ethnicity. Through the war in Croatia in 1991, as I already said, the division was completed in practical terms. After that, notably from 1992 onwards, that is to say towards 1993 and 1994, the term "the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina" is one that sounds absurd to me, because Bosnia-Herzegovina consists of three constituent peoples, all of them being equal. I think that often one tends to forget that Mr. Izetbegovic, in the autumn of 1992, under circumstances that were unclear, continued his term as President. I have the impression that throughout this war conflict, the Muslim side, later the Bosniak side, found that position to be very important. It so happened that they had maintained Sarajevo, under siege in all fairness, as their administrative centre of the former republic, Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to everything that happened afterwards, the HVO was treated as part of the single armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Practically, they do not come to life until 1994, and then at a rather low level but after some pressure was brought to bear by certain circles outside, that is to say from the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, was it the joint forces that did not come to life before 1994? I'm referring to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO as the armed forces of then Bosnia-Herzegovina? Or was it only the HVO that did not manage to fit into these joint forces? Or was it that the authorities from Sarajevo did not recognise it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: The authorities from Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who were these authorities from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Purely Muslim authorities. Bosniak, rather. I explained, using the example of the Supreme Command staff, its cosmetic role at that with other ethnicities. Well, even this agreement dated the 21st of July, 1992, between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HVO was defined as part of the armed forces. However, the two were never fused. I am quoting a letter that refers to that dating back to sometime in October, 1992. It was signed by the head of staff of the HVO, Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic. He presents most of the reasons why this did not occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please, I shall be very brief. I would like to refer to three further questions which are very important to my mind, and I think that until the present day, they are not fully clear to all of us here. We mentioned the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did it ever exist? And if so, since when? And when did it not exist? The government of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This is always a question. When a certain government is constituted on the basis of certain principles, certain tenets, this government of the last Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, after October, 1990, was constituted by the representatives of the three peoples. At the beginning of 1992, the representatives of the Serb people walked out of it and they established a government of their own. From then onwards, we can say that the government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a rump government, which is what occurred in 1991. It is similar, of course, to what happened to the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It was not recognised, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I would like you to clarify something else for this honourable Trial Chamber. The Prosecution has been claiming here that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina today - today - exists as it existed then. And they always say what the source is. They always say the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina provided such and such a thing for us. After Dayton, after 1995, is there a government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, as for the subject matter of Bosnia-Herzegovina after the Dayton Accords is something that I have not been dealing with. I'm interested in the war. What is going on there today is something that is a protectorate of the international community, and I've already stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Since you do not deal in this subject matter I'm not going to ask you about this. And do you know that until Dayton, until 1995, the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I think that I saw one or two rulings of this Court, annulling the decision on the SAO Krajinas and the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know which year this is?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: I think that it's the end of 1992 but I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, was there a constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina at all at that time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Well, look, there is obviously something that is given that title. The question is, after the Serbs and the Croats parted ways with them, the question is what remained of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I have a final question. You mentioned the AID today. Can you tell the honourable Trial Chamber what you know about the AID as an historian; what's its role? What is it? And while working as an historian, I assume that you are involved in discovering forgeries. To the best of my understanding, history focuses on sources and they are the most important.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So what can you tell the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I have one final question and then you ask about -- we all --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, you're right. I'll take them one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: First of all, what do you know about the AID, the Agency for Investigations and Documentation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: As far as I know, my knowledge about that institution is primarily of a secondary nature, so from the point of view of an historian, they are of lesser importance. It is primarily through the press and the recollections of political and military factors, leaders from Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is why I shall be using the term "allegedly" here. It is claimed in respect of that institution that it was established --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We are now, by the witness's own testimony just now, all he's going to do apparently is relate to the Chamber allegations that somebody else has made. That's not proper evidence under any Tribunal rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, I think the question you asked is out of the scope of this expertise of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I agree, if the AID is part of history. However, historians deal with history and the AID is in history and, thank God, it was abolished a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I thought that as part of history --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think statements by counsel and personal opinions by counsel are proper either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Neither did I. Well, Mr. Krsnik, the problem of this testimony is that he said that his knowledge is of secondary nature. He has no direct knowledge of the role, function of the AID, and he is an expert of history. So we kindly ask you to skip this question. Let us come to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know if we have understood each other properly. My main question refers to sources that are the most important thing for any historian's work. I am referring to sources. The expert mentioned today, when answering the questions put by my learned friend, that these were forgeries, fabrications, by the AID. Judge Clark is right, as usual. I put many questions within one question. I tried precisely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, if you have the hard evidence to show that a particular document is a forgery, and that this expert witness have something to do with that document, you may ask your questions in that direction. Otherwise, you will get us nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Mr. President. Then I would kindly ask the expert to explain to the honourable Trial Chamber what he meant when answering Mr. Seric's question when he said that the attack on Prozor and everything that followed is something that was fabricated by the AID.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: This story was put on paper. And this was done by the already-mentioned Institute for Investigating Genocide. The documents that it has at its disposal are treated, particularly in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, because all the agencies were created according to the same pattern, so they are treated as strictly confidential. Such documents, irrespective of their authors, are inaccessible for a period of 30 to 50 years. On the other hand, the institute, in its work, in its books, invokes a large number of statements. For such a quantity of statements, a humungous staff is required and the institute does not have such resources. On the other hand, irrespective of its name, the institute is involved in Muslim victims only. And over the past days or, rather, over the past months, some indictments were issued in Sarajevo as well, and it is stated in the press, publicly, that the AID is behind that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the arrest of the director of AID and his colleagues?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN
utterances.text: No, no. I'm thinking about some indictments against Serbs, where people admitted to the murders of people who are alive. I mean, people who were later found to be still alive. This matter was very widely written about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness, and I am hoping that your testimony has contributed to our search for the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we only have less than 15 minutes left for this morning's sitting, and we decided to have an early recess today because we believe that 15 minutes will get the Prosecution nowhere and we will keep his cross-examination intact. Another thing is that, as for the documents D2/72 and 73, we are expecting the English translations so that tomorrow afternoon, the Judges and the Prosecution won't be at a disadvantaged position. Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have a suggestion, and please decide. If the Prosecution has documents to show to this gentleman, and if it is a lot, that requires a lot of reading, perhaps we could provide the expert witness with the opportunity that he can read that so that tomorrow, during the cross-examination, we don't needs to make breaks in order for him to go through the documents. This is my suggestion and I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott? Any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we decline that invitation. We will present our cross-examination exhibits at the beginning of cross-examination. And after today, with getting into so many new areas, I can tell the Chamber now there will be substantial work on documents overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But you promise to furnish all those documents tomorrow afternoon before the beginning of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the beginning of the cross-examination, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'm sorry to tell you that we have to keep you here in The Hague for another day at least. You have to remember that during your stay here, you are still under the oath. So please do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will resume tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 1.34 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of September, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
